Rate Limits and Timeouts — Ramp API docs

Rate Limits and Timeouts

## Request timeouts

A 504 Gateway Timeout means a gateway did not receive an upstream response before its timeout. Avoid relying on long-running requests when working with large datasets or complex queries:

- Use pagination to break large requests into smaller chunks.
- Retry reads with exponential backoff after a `504`. Before retrying a write, check whether it completed and follow the endpoint's idempotency behavior; a timeout does not prove the operation failed.

## Rate limiting

The standard Developer API limit is 200 requests per 10 seconds per source IP address. Requests from integrations that share an outbound IP share this limit. Approved higher limits may differ.

Production token issuance has an additional limit: 100 `POST /developer/v1/token` requests per 10 seconds per source IP. Reuse access tokens until they expire rather than requesting a token for each API call.

Exceeding a limit returns 429 Too Many Requests and can block subsequent requests for 60 seconds. A 10-second counting period does not mean access resumes 10 seconds after a burst.

## Tips for handling rate limits

- Honor `Retry-After` when present. Otherwise, use exponential backoff with jitter and allow for the rate-limit cooldown. Avoid immediate retries.
- Coordinate callers sharing an IP. Budget requests across workers and integrations, including token requests.
- Reduce unnecessary requests. Cache data where appropriate, reuse tokens, and use pagination or supported batch operations.

## Requesting higher limits

If your application requires a higher limit, you can request an increase. To do so:

1. Analyze and document your expected API usage.
2. Submit a Developer API support ticket with your account details and usage requirements.

Providing clear information about your use case and anticipated volume will help expedite the review process.

## Syncing data

Pagination is the mechanism for moving through a result set, but building a reliable sync pipeline also requires knowing which records to fetch and how often. This section covers how to do an initial bulk pull and keep your local data up to date efficiently.

### Initial seed pull

The first time you sync a dataset, you will need to paginate through all records without any date filter. Expect this to be slow for large datasets — a business with years of transaction history may require hundreds of requests.

Recommendation: persist the data locally (in a database or cache) rather than fetching it on every app load. Once you have a local copy, you only need to fetch new or changed records on subsequent syncs.

### Incremental sync strategies

After the initial seed, store the timestamp of your last successful sync and use an available date filter where its meaning matches your use case. A creation-date filter only finds newly created records. The transaction `synced_after` filter only finds transactions that have been synced to an accountin

Webhooks — Ramp API docs

Webhooks

## Overview

Webhooks allow your application to receive real-time notifications about events that occur in your Ramp account. Instead of polling our API, webhooks push notifications to your specified endpoint whenever an event happens.

Key benefits:

- Instant notification of events like transactions, approvals, or reimbursements
- Reduces the need for polling APIs to check for updates
- Enables automation of downstream workflows (e.g., syncing with accounting software)

Ramp also exposes an inbound webhook endpoint for AI platforms that broadcast customer usage events into Ramp. If your product lets customers bring their Ramp API key and receive model, token, cost, and attribution data in Ramp, see AI Usage Tracking. That endpoint uses `POST /developer/v1/ai-usage/unified` and does not require a webhook subscription through `POST /developer/v1/webhooks`.

## Available events

Permanent link: Available events

Subscribe to the event types below for business workflows. Where a public OAuth scope is available, request the scope for the underlying resource so your integration can read the object after receiving the event.

Authorization — Ramp API docs

Authorization

Ramp uses OAuth 2.0. Your app gets an access token from `/developer/v1/token`, authenticating with its client ID and secret (typically HTTP Basic Auth), and scopes control what the token can access.

For a quick start, see the Setup Guide. For Ramp's own MCP server and CLI, see Ramp MCP and Ramp CLI.

## Supported grant types

| Grant Type | Use Case | User Interaction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client Credentials | Internal integrations, server-to-server | None required |
| Authorization Code | Third-party apps, public integrations | Authorized user consent required |
| Refresh Token | Renew access after an Authorization Code grant | None after the initial authorization |

## Permission model and scopes

Scopes follow the pattern `resource:permission`, where the permission is usually `read` or `write`, such as `transactions:read`. A few use other permissions, such as `cards:read_vault`. OpenID Connect scopes, such as `openid` and `offline_access`, don't follow the pattern.

Request only the scopes your app needs. Each endpoint's API reference lists its required scopes. The table below lists common scopes and isn't exhaustive.

| Scope | Resource | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `accounting:read` | Accounting data | Access accounting sync status and metadata |
| `accounting:write` | Accounting data | Update accounting sync settings and connections |
| `ai_spend:read` | AI spend | View AI token usage and spend data |
| `ai_spend:write` | AI spend | Update AI spend and tagging settings |
| `ai_usage:write` | AI usage | Report AI and LLM usage data for spend tracking |
| `applications:read` | Applications | View financing application status (partners only) |
| `applications:write` | Applications | Requested in the application OAuth consent flow; not required to submit applications (partners only) |
| `approvals:read` | Approvals | View approval data for transactions, reimbursements, and bills |
| `approvals:write` | Approvals | Approve or reject pending approvals |
| `audit_logs:read` | Audit logs | View business audit log events |
| `bank_accounts:read` | Bank accounts | View connected bank account information |
| `bank_accounts:write` | Bank accounts | Create and manage bank account information (partners only) |
| `billing_statements:read` | Billing statements | View your Ramp billing statements |
| `bills:read` | Bills | Access bill data and payment history |
| `bills:write` | Bills | Create, update, and pay bills |
| `blank_canvas:write` | Blank canvas approvals | Approve, reject, and update external workflow steps |
| `budgets:read` | Budgets | View budget information |
| `business:read` | Business profile | Access business information and settings |
| `cards:read` | Cards | View physical and virtual card information |
| `cards:read_vault` | Card vault | Access sensitive card data (PAN, CVV) |
| `cards:write` | Cards | Create, update, and manage cards |
| `cashbacks:read` | Cashback rewards | View

Welcome — Ramp API docs

## Get started

Use Ramp at your company, or build for others.

For customers

Have a Ramp account? Create credentials and make your first API call.

For partners

Building an integration for other businesses? Start with the partner program.

Get sandbox access

Don't have a Ramp account? Request a sandbox to start building right away.

## Use cases

End-to-end build journeys that span multiple Ramp products.

AI Agents

Connect agents to Ramp via MCP or the CLI. Read data, process approvals, make purchases.

AI Usage Tracking

Let customers connect Ramp, then broadcast their AI usage events into Ramp spend analytics.

Applications

Partner-led customer onboarding. Pre-fill a Ramp application, optionally request OAuth consent, track status via webhooks.

Bill Payments

Create approved bills via API and pay vendors end-to-end. Pick a payment method, attach docs, run 3-way match.

Customized Approvers

Route approvals based on accounting dimensions via matrix tables.

ERP Integrations

Two-way sync between Ramp and your customer ERP — chart of accounts in, transactions and bills out.

Procurement Integrations with the Blank Canvas API

Receive Ramp intake requests in your tool and return approval decisions via Blank Canvas.

Spend programs

The recurring-budget pattern. Mint funds from a template so policy stays consistent.

User lifecycle

Onboard, update, deactivate, reactivate, and stage draft users via the API.

Agent Payments

Choose Agent Cards, Stripe MPP, or x402 for an agent purchase.

## Products

Editorial hubs for each Ramp product surface — concepts, mental model, where to go next.

AI Index

Business AI adoption by vendor, industry sector, and company size.

Bill Pay Bills, draft bills, payments, vendors, 3-way match.

Cards

Virtual, physical, and agent cards. Every card draws against a fund.

Custom Records Define your own data model in Ramp.

Procurement Intake requests, purchase orders, vendor onboarding.

Ramp Rate

Software adoption and growth benchmarks across categories and vendors.

Reimbursements

Out-of-pocket employee expenses — manual, OCR-drafted receipts, mileage.

Spend Controls

Funds, spend programs, and approvals — the policy layer behind every dollar.

Users

The people on a Ramp account. Status, identity, async creation.

## Conventions

API rules and cross-cutting patterns. Reference while building.

Data relationships How Ramp resources connect to each other.

Deferred tasks Async work, polling, lifecycle.

Errors Status codes, error shapes, debugging.

Monetary values Currency, precision, ISO codes.

Pagination Cursor-based, page sizes, sort order.

Rate limits and timeouts Quotas, backoff, headers to read.

Support

Grab the x-trace-id, follow the trace, file a developer support ticket.

Webhooks Subscribe, verify signatures, retry.

Canonical OpenAPI schema for the Developer API: /openapi/developer-api.json.

Ramp MCP — Ramp API docs

Ramp MCP

Ramp MCP connects AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor to your Ramp account. Each connection acts as the signed-in user, with that user's Ramp permissions.

## Connect

- Claude: Install Ramp from Claude's directory↗, then sign in to Ramp.
- ChatGPT: Install Ramp from the ChatGPT app directory↗.
- Cursor: Add Ramp to Cursor with one click.
- Claude Code:

Shell

Copy

claude mcp add --transport http ramp https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp

- Codex:

Shell

codex mcp add ramp --url https://mcp.ramp.com/mcp

- Other clients: Coding agents can also use Ramp CLI. For other MCP clients, gateways, and the sandbox, see Connect to Ramp↗.

When you sign in, choose Full access or Read-only. Connections expire after 30 days; reconnect to renew.

## Connection issues

- "The app you are using is not currently supported" means your client's redirect URI isn't allowlisted. Request a redirect URI.
- You can't connect at all: your Ramp role may not include access to AI tools. Ask your Admin; see Manage connected AI tools↗.

For the full tool list and more troubleshooting, see Connect to Ramp↗ and the Agent tools reference↗.

# Help: PitchBook API

Find information about PitchBook’s API solution and discover how it can meet your business needs. Our API is a separate offering from the PitchBook Platform that requires a standalone contract agreement.

## Overview

PitchBook’s API solution allows you to call specific PitchBook data into your internal business systems on demand. This flexible solution means you have access to PitchBook’s expansive database. It’s the ideal integration for CRM enrichment, allowing you to extract data on an ad-hoc basis that meets the needs of your organization.

You can explore a specific entity and retrieve valuable data, and the API solution enables you to apply specific criteria, such as location and industry, to drill down into the businesses you discover.

## Use cases

The API is a good solution if:

- Your scope and data points are subject to change frequently.
- You require a near-instant population of data.
- You perform ad-hoc research.
- You want to see past and present financial data.
- RESTful API is a system requirement.

## How the API works

Accessing the API

The PitchBook API is a RESTful implementation that most HTTP clients can easily access in your chosen language or via a web browser. Every call will use the same base URL: https://api.pitchbook.com

Available data points

The API solution offers a variety of relational endpoints, including financing details, deal stock information, as well as AI-powered VC exit predictor data. See the full list from our API Endpoints Overview document.

Create your API connection

To start your API connection, you will need to send a request directly to our Direct Data team through this link.

Or if you’re a PitchBook client, you can also head to the Plugins & Apps section from the My PitchBook section of the left-hand sidebar on the PitchBook Platform and choose PitchBook API.

![Plugins and apps section of left-hand side-bar.jpg](https://pitchbook.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/de1a7a4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1000x626+0+0/resize/1000x626!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fk2-prod-pitchbook-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8b%2F31%2F26280cf44004aa914076f6bf50ac%2Fplugins-and-apps-section-of-left-hand-side-bar.jpg)

From this section on the platform, you can test specific endpoints. This section on PitchBook also allows you to reach out to our Direct Data team to request access to the API.

## Next steps

Our team will work with you to understand the insights and data you’re looking for and help you establish the API connection through an API key or authentication token. Available data for each entity type is packaged across several endpoints so you can map the data to your desired format and structure.

 Authentication

The Gemini Notebook API uses OAuth 2.0 to authenticate requests on behalf of a Google user. Every request must include an OAuth 2.0 Bearer token in the `Authorization` HTTP header. The API doesn't accept API keys.

## Before you begin Copy link to this section: Before you begin

- Create or select a Google Cloud project. You enable the API, configure the OAuth consent screen, and create OAuth clients in this project. To create a project, see Create a Google Cloud project.
- Use a personal Google Account. During the Public Preview, the Gemini Notebook API is only available for personal Google Accounts. Requests authenticated with a Google Workspace account fail with `403 PERMISSION_DENIED` (`WORKSPACE_ACCOUNT_NOT_SUPPORTED`).
- Sign in to Gemini Notebook once. The API reads and writes the notebooks of the authorizing user, so each Google Account must have signed in to Gemini Notebook at least once before calling the API. If an account has never signed in to Gemini Notebook, `CreateNotebook` requests fail with `404 NOT_FOUND` (`Account not found for user.`).

Copy link to this section: OAuth 2.0 scopes

| Scope | Access | Supported methods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/notebook` | Read and write access to notebooks and sources | `CreateNotebook`, `GetNotebook`, `ListNotebooks`, `UpdateNotebook`, `CreateSource`, `UploadSource`, `GetSource`, `ListSources` |

Help me connect to the remote Gemini Notebook MCP server (`https://notebook.googleapis.com/mcp`). Follow these exact steps:

1. Check if `gcloud` is installed and ask me which Google Cloud PROJECT_ID to use (you can list my projects with `gcloud projects list --limit=10` or check `gcloud config get-value project`).

```
sources.page_content:
Rate limits and quotas | Gemini Notebook API | Google for Developers

 Rate limits and quotas

The Gemini Notebook API is free to use during the Public Preview period, subject to the following request rate limits and account capacity quotas.

## Request rate limits Copy link to this section: Request rate limits

Rate limits are enforced both per Google Cloud project and per authenticated Google user:

### Per-project rate limits Copy link to this section: Per-project rate limits

| Quota metric | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Read requests (`GetNotebook`, `ListNotebooks`, `GetSource`, `ListSources`) | 100 requests per minute (RPM) per project |
| Write requests (`CreateNotebook`, `UpdateNotebook`, `CreateSource`, `UploadSource`) | 100 requests per minute (RPM) per project |

### Per-user rate limits Copy link to this section: Per-user rate limits

| Method | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| `CreateSource` | 20 requests per minute (RPM) per user |
| `UploadSource` | 20 uploads per minute per user |
| All other methods (`CreateNotebook`, `GetNotebook`, `ListNotebooks`, `UpdateNotebook`, `GetSource`, `ListSources`) | 60 requests per minute (RPM) per user per method |

When a rate limit is exceeded, the API returns HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` (`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`). Retry failed requests using exponential backoff with jitter. For `UploadSource`, the error includes a `RetryInfo` with the delay before you can start another upload.

## Source size limits

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Maximum source length | 500,000 words per source |
| Maximum inline `text_content` payload size | 1,000,000 bytes (1 MB) |
| Maximum uploaded file size (`UploadSource`) | 200 MiB (209,715,200 bytes) |
| Maximum notebook or source `displayName` length | 500 characters |

## Account tier quotas

Maximum notebook and source counts depend on the authenticated user's subscription tier:

| Tier | Maximum notebooks per user | Maximum sources per notebook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | 100 | 50 |
| Plus | 200 | 100 |
| Pro | 500 | 300 |
| Ultra | 500 | 600 |
```

# Workspace Webhooks 

Otter Help

 October 29, 2026 20:58 Updated 

Workspace Admins can set up webhooks for your workspace so you can integrate Otter Conversation data into your downstream tools and workflows.

## Webhook Payload

Key Fields

- abstract_summary: A concise summary of the meeting’s essential details
- action_items: The list of AI-detected tasks and responsibilities assigned to participants
- insights: A detailed breakdown of key topics and points discussed
- outline: Custom topics or questions to extract precise information from the meeting
- transcript: Contains the entire transcript of the meeting
- calendar_guests: The emails of the users invited to the calendar event (if exists)

 Tip: Use `calendar_guests` to match contacts in external systems (for example, syncing meeting participants to your CRM)
- conf_join_url: Join URL for the associated meeting (Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, etc.), if available
- owner: The Otter user who owns the conversation
- shared_emails: List of users or email addresses the conversation is shared with, including permission levels
- shared_channels: List of channels the conversation is shared with, including channel details (such as name, member count, and discoverability) and permission levels

# Otter.ai Public API 

Otter Help

 October 29, 2026 20:46 Updated 

Otter.ai’s Public API provides programmatic access to retrieve channels, conversations, transcripts, audio, action items, insights, outlines, and workspace details from your Otter account.

 Getting Started: Otter's Public API is available for all Enterprise workspaces. If you do not see this feature for your workspace, contact your Otter account manager.

## API Fundamentals

Essential information for authenticating, paging through results, and understanding usage limits.

## Authentication Create and manage your API keys 

All API requests require authentication using Bearer token authentication. Follow the steps below to create your API key. 

1. Go to Integrations → Developer. ![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/44608393062679)
2. Click Create key.

![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/36793479454359)
3. Click Copy and store the API key in a safe place.

 Note: This is only visible once. Make sure you copy the API key in this pop-up. If you forget to copy, follow steps 1-3 to create another key.

![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/36793479455255)
4. The API key can now be used. Follow steps 1-4 to create another API key.

 Note: There is a limit of 2 API keys per user.

![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/44608393063831)

Using your API key:

Include your API key in the Authorization header for every request:

```plaintext
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
```

✅ Security best practices:

- Never share your API key publicly or commit it to version control
- Store API keys securely using environment variables or secrets management
- Rotate API keys periodically

## Rate Limits

Enterprise plan users are currently limited to 10 requests / second. If you exceed your rate limit, you'll receive a `429 Too Many Requests` response.

## Pagination

List endpoints use cursor-based pagination for efficient data retrieval.

### Pagination Response

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "retrieved_at": "2025-07-31T12:00:00Z",
    "has_more": true,
    "next_cursor": "next_cursor_position"
  },
  "data": [ /* array of results */ ]
}
```

Meta Fields:

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `retrieved_at` | string | Timestamp when data was retrieved (ISO 8601 format) |
| `has_more` | boolean | Whether more pages are available |
| `next_cursor` | string (optional) | Cursor for the next page |

### Usage

To retrieve the next page, use the `next_cursor` value in your next request's `cursor` query parameter:

```plaintext
GET /conversations?cursor=next_cursor_position&limit=20
```

Continue paginating until `has_more` is `false`.

## Webhooks

Webhooks are the recommended way to build export integrations with Otter. Instead of constantly polling the API to check for new conversations or action items, webhooks push real-time notifications to your application the moment events occur. This makes webhooks

- action_items: The list of AI-detected tasks and responsibilities assigned to participants
- insights: A detailed breakdown of key topics and points discussed
- outline: Custom topics or questions to extract precise information from the meeting
- transcript: Contains the entire transcript of the meeting
- calendar_guests: The emails of the users invited to the calendar event (if exists)

 Tip: Use `calendar_guests` to match contacts in external systems (for example, syncing meeting participants to your CRM)
- conf_join_url: Join URL for the associated meeting (Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, etc.), if available
- owner: The Otter user who owns the conversation
- shared_emails: List of users or email addresses the conversation is shared with, including permission levels
- shared_channels: List of channels the conversation is shared with, including channel details (such as name, member count, and discoverability) and permission levels

Otter.ai Public API – Help Center

# Otter.ai Public API 

Otter Help

 October 29, 2026 20:46 Updated 

Otter.ai’s Public API provides programmatic access to retrieve channels, conversations, transcripts, audio, action items, insights, outlines, and workspace details from your Otter account.

 Getting Started: Otter's Public API is available for all Enterprise workspaces. If you do not see this feature for your workspace, contact your Otter account manager.

## API Fundamentals

Essential information for authenticating, paging through results, and understanding usage limits.

## Authentication Create and manage your API keys 

All API requests require authentication using Bearer token authentication. Follow the steps below to create your API key. 

1. Go to Integrations → Developer. ![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/44608393062679)
2. Click Create key.

![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/36793479454359)
3. Click Copy and store the API key in a safe place.

 Note: This is only visible once. Make sure you copy the API key in this pop-up. If you forget to copy, follow steps 1-3 to create another key.

![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/36793479455255)
4. The API key can now be used. Follow steps 1-4 to create another API key.

 Note: There is a limit of 2 API keys per user.

![](https://help.otter.ai/hc/article_attachments/44608393063831)

Using your API key:

Include your API key in the Authorization header for every request:

```plaintext
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
```

✅ Security best practices:

- Never share your API key publicly or commit it to version control
- Store API keys securely using environment variables or secrets management
- Rotate API keys periodically

## Rate Limits

Enterprise plan users are currently limited to 10 requests / second. If you exceed your rate limit, you'll receive a `429 Too Many Requests` response.

## Pagination

List endpoints use cursor-based pagination for efficient data retrieval.

### Pagination Response

```json
{
  "meta": {
    "retrieved_at": "2025-07-31T12:00:00Z",
    "has_more": true,
    "next_cursor": "next_cursor_position"
  },
  "data": [ /* array of results */ ]
}
```

Meta Fields:

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `retrieved_at` | string | Timestamp when data was retrieved (ISO 8601 format) |
| `has_more` | boolean | Whether more pages are available |
| `next_cursor` | string (optional) | Cursor for the next page |

### Usage

To retrieve the next page, use the `next_cursor` value in your next request's `cursor` query parameter:

```plaintext
GET /conversations?cursor=next_cursor_position&limit=20
```

Continue paginating until `has_more` is `false`.

## Webhooks

Webhooks are the recommended way to build export integrations with Otter. Instead of constantly polling the API to check for new conversations or action items, webhooks push real-time notifications to your application the moment events occur. This makes webhooks

Public API

# Public API

Edited

 Wednesday, November 12 2025

Fathom now has a public API that gives you developer‑friendly access to meeting insights so you can build workflows and integrations that connect Fathom with the rest of your tools.

- Build exactly what you need - bring meeting summaries, transcripts, and action items right into your own tools and workflows for a tailored experience.
- Save time with automation - automate repetitive post‑meeting tasks and cut out manual copy‑paste so work moves faster.
- Unlock more use cases - extend Fathom with third‑party apps and integrations, opening the door to new org‑wide use cases.

### Who this is for

- Anyone can browse the API docs and start building!
- Partners can register an OAuth app to be eligible for a future marketplace listing as a Fathom‑approved integration.

### How to get started

- Looking for plug‑and‑play integrations? Visit the Integration Hub.
- Building internal workflows? Start with the Quickstart Guide.
- Publishing an integration for customers? Create an OAuth app here.

### Keep in mind

- API keys and access: API keys are created at the user level. Your key can access meetings recorded by you or shared to your Team. Admin API keys do not grant access to other users’ unshared meetings.
- Rate Limiting: users can make 60 calls per minute across all of their API keys; this ensures system stability and reliability. With that in mind, we do not offer higher rate limits at this time. 

If you have any questions, reach out to help@fathom.video. We’re happy to assist!

# Use Consensus in ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or with the API

> Connect Consensus to ChatGPT, Claude, or Microsoft 365 Copilot in one click, or build on it with the API, so answers cite real peer-reviewed papers.

If you already use ChatGPT, Claude, or Microsoft 365 Copilot, connect Consensus to it. Your assistant can then search over 400 million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, apply academic filters, hand research questions to the Consensus research agent, and cite real research instead of answering from memory.

## Connect in one click

Pick your assistant and add Consensus from its app directory.

> [card] ChatGPT
> 
> Add Consensus from the ChatGPT app directory.

> [card] Claude
> 
> Add Consensus from the Claude connectors directory.

> [card] Microsoft 365 Copilot
> 
> Add Consensus for Copilot from the Microsoft Marketplace.

Sign in with your Consensus account the first time you connect. Your results depend on your Consensus plan, not your ChatGPT, Claude, or Copilot subscription.

### Connect another tool

Using a different assistant or tool, such as Cursor, VS Code, or Claude Code? Connect it to the Consensus MCP server directly. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for AI assistants to use outside tools. The server is hosted, so there's nothing to install:

```text
https://mcp.consensus.app/mcp

```

> [card] Set up your client
> 
> Step-by-step connection guides for Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini Spark, Copilot Studio, and any other MCP client.

## What your assistant can do

Search. The `search` tool returns ranked papers with title, authors, journal, publication year, citation count, study type, a key takeaway, and a link to the paper on Consensus. On paid plans it also returns query-relevant excerpts from open-access papers, so your assistant can quote the passage behind each claim. Your assistant can pass the same filters Research Agent uses:

- Year range, study type, and journal quartile (SJR)
- Human and controlled studies, minimum sample size, minimum citations
- Medical mode, open access only, exclude preprints
- Study duration and country

Read whole papers. On paid plans, `get_full_text` reads the complete text of open-access papers from search results or Threads, so your assistant can work from a paper's methods and results, not just its abstract.

Threads. With a signed-in account, your assistant can also run Research Agent as a Thread. `create_thread` starts the agent on a research question, `get_thread` returns the cited answer when it's ready, `add_to_thread` asks a follow-up, and `find_threads` finds earlier Threads. The agent can search your Library collections and save papers to them, and `deep` mode runs a longer literature review on paid plans.

> [card] Quick start:

# Start building with the Consensus API and MCP

> Pick a surface, run your first filtered search, and find the guide for what you are building.

Four steps from zero to a working integration.

1. Pick your surface

Use MCP to try Consensus inside Claude or ChatGPT in two minutes, or when each person should search under their own account. Use the API for anything in code — monitoring agents, literature tables, pipelines, and scientific agents running on one shared key.

2. Run one filtered search

Make your first request, then add filters one at a time. The filters are where precision comes from.

```bash
curl -G "https://api.consensus.app/v1/search" -H "x-api-key: $CONSENSUS_API_KEY" \
  --data-urlencode "query=vision-language models for robot manipulation" \
  --data-urlencode "domain=cs" \
  --data-urlencode "year_min=2024"

```

3. Read the guide for what you are building

Start with internal tools or research systems, then read best practices for rate limits, pagination, and grounding rules.

4. Scale up when you need to

Enterprise adds up to 1,000 results per request, custom call volumes, and custom rate limits. Talk to us about a trial.

## Next

> [card] Build internal research tools
> 
> Assistants, field-monitoring agents, literature tables, and scientific agents.

> [card] Build custom research systems
> 
> Literature reviews, grounded writing, and evidence reports.

> ## Documentation Index
> 
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.consensus.app/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# API plans and access

> What each Consensus plan includes on the API: monthly calls, papers per request, pagination, full-text excerpts, complete text, citations, and rate limits.

The API is self-serve on every Consensus plan. Your plan sets how many calls you get each month, how many papers each request can return, and which features you can use.

## Get a key

1. Open the dashboard

Sign in to Consensus and go to consensus.app/api-mcp, or click your profile icon and choose API & MCP Dashboard.

2. Create a key

Click Create API key, name it, and copy it. If you already have a key, open Keys and clients and click New key. The full key is shown once.

3. Send it on every request

Pass the key in the `x-api-key` header. Requests without a valid key return `401`.

## What each plan includes

| | Free | Pro | Teams | Deep | Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Included calls per month | 30 | 500 | 500 | 2,000 | Custom |
| Max calls with additional usage | 30 | 1,000 | 1,000 | 10,000 | Custom |
| Max papers per request (`page_size`) | 20 | 300 | 300 | 750 | 1,000 |
| Pagination past the first page | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Full-text excerpts | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Complete text of open-access papers** | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Institutional full-text links (`institutional_access_url`)* | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Citations and references (beta)*** | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Rate limit | 1 request/second | 1 request/second | 1 request/second | 1 request/second | Custom |

* Returned on the first 50 search results and on Thread citations when you've selected your institution in Consensus settings. An organization key uses the institution of the person who created it.

** `GET /v1/papers/full_text`, at 1 credit per paper returned.

*** `GET /v1beta/papers/citations` and `GET /v1beta/papers/references`, at 1 credit per 100 papers returned. Both are in beta, so their request and response schemas may change in the coming days.

Every plan can use every search filter. Compare plans at consensus.app/pricing.

## How calls are counted

- One call per 100 papers returned, rounded up, with a minimum of one call per request. A request that returns 20 papers is 1 call; 150 papers is 2 calls.
- A Thread is charged by the amount of work the agent does. `mode` controls the effort: a `deep` run does more work than a `pro` run, so it costs more. A failed run costs nothing. While a Thread runs, its maximum possible cost counts as used. If that doesn't fit under your plan's limit, creating the Thread or adding a follow-up returns `429`.
- One credit per full text returned. Complete text costs 1 credit for each paper whose Markdown comes back, and a credit counts the same as a call. Papers that come back blocked or not found cost nothing

> ## Documentation Index
> 
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.consensus.app/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Use Consensus in ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or with the API

> Connect Consensus to ChatGPT, Claude, or Microsoft 365 Copilot in one click, or build on it with the API, so answers cite real peer-reviewed papers.

If you already use ChatGPT, Claude, or Microsoft 365 Copilot, connect Consensus to it. Your assistant can then search over 400 million scholarly articles, including 350 million peer-reviewed research papers, apply academic filters, hand research questions to the Consensus research agent, and cite real research instead of answering from memory.

## Connect in one click

Pick your assistant and add Consensus from its app directory.

> [card] ChatGPT
> 
> Add Consensus from the ChatGPT app directory.

> [card] Claude
> 
> Add Consensus from the Claude connectors directory.

> [card] Microsoft 365 Copilot
> 
> Add Consensus for Copilot from the Microsoft Marketplace.

Sign in with your Consensus account the first time you connect. Your results depend on your Consensus plan, not your ChatGPT, Claude, or Copilot subscription.

### Connect another tool

Using a different assistant or tool, such as Cursor, VS Code, or Claude Code? Connect it to the Consensus MCP server directly. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for AI assistants to use outside tools. The server is hosted, so there's nothing to install:

```text
https://mcp.consensus.app/mcp

```

> [card] Set up your client
> 
> Step-by-step connection guides for Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, Gemini Spark, Copilot Studio, and any other MCP client.

## What your assistant can do

Search. The `search` tool returns ranked papers with title, authors, journal, publication year, citation count, study type, a key takeaway, and a link to the paper on Consensus. On paid plans it also returns query-relevant excerpts from open-access papers, so your assistant can quote the passage behind each claim. Your assistant can pass the same filters Research Agent uses:

- Year range, study type, and journal quartile (SJR)
- Human and controlled studies, minimum sample size, minimum citations
- Medical mode, open access only, exclude preprints
- Study duration and country

Read whole papers. On paid plans, `get_full_text` reads the complete text of open-access papers from search results or Threads, so your assistant can work from a paper's methods and results, not just its abstract.

Threads. With a signed-in account, your assistant can also run Research Agent as a Thread. `create_thread` starts the agent on a research question, `get_thread` returns the cited answer when it's ready, `add_to_thread` asks a follow-up, and `find_threads` finds earlier Threads. The agent can search your Library collections and save papers to them, and `deep` mode runs a longer literature review on paid plans.

# Usage and Pricing

Reducto measures usage separately for each product. Your contract and rate card is the source of truth. Contracted customers may have negotiated rates that differ from the list prices below.

Once installed, agents in Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, or any other Model Context Protocol client can classify, parse, extract, split, and edit documents as part of their reasoning loop, without custom integration code.

```bash
uvx mcp-server-reducto --login

```

Codex

```toml
command = "uvx"
args = ["mcp-server-reducto"]

```

```json
    "reducto": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.reducto.ai/mcp",

      }
```

# Rate Limits

> Note: Legacy Parse uses a different concurrency model. See Concurrency Throttle (Legacy).

## Page Concurrency

Page concurrency is the number of pages of your r-1 and r-1 mini jobs that Reducto processes at the same time for your account. Pages above the limit wait in a queue, and Reducto processes them as soon as capacity is available.

### r-1

| Tier | US | EU |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard | 500 | 250 |
| Growth | 2,000 | 1,000 |
| Enterprise | 4,000+ | 2,000+ |

### r-1 mini

| Tier | US | EU |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard | 50 | 25 |
| Growth | 1,000 | 500 |
| Enterprise | 2,000+ | 1,000+ |

Enterprise accounts can get custom caps. Contact sales (support@reducto.ai) to discuss.

US is the default region. The EU column applies to requests that you send to the EU region. All values are in pages of your jobs in progress at the same time.

## Limit Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Applies to | What it limits | When you exceed it | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Page concurrency | r-1 and r-1 mini jobs | Pages in progress at the same time for your account | Work waits in a queue, then runs | `200` (after wait) |
| Edge rate limits | Every request | Requests per second for each API key | Reducto rejects the request at the ingress | `429` |
| Sync connections | Sync requests (`/parse`, `/extract`, `/split`) | Open connections that wait for a result. Keep at most 50 to 200 at the same time, and use async for more. | The connection stays open until the job completes, up to the 15-minute (900s) timeout | `200`, or a timeout |
| Concurrency throttle (legacy) | Legacy Parse jobs | Parse batches in progress at the same time for your account | Work waits in a queue, then runs | `200` (after wait) |

## How Page Concurrency Works

- Work above the cap waits. Reducto queues the extra work and runs it when other work completes. You see added latency, not a `429`.
- Higher limits. If your tail latency increases at high volume, the cause is work that waits in the queue. Contact sales (support@reducto.ai) for higher limits.

# API Quickstart

## Prerequisites

### Create a Reducto account

Sign up for a free account without leaving the docs.

You need a Reducto account. Sign up or sign in at https://studio.reducto.ai. Signed-in readers see their account and organization here.

### Get your API key

Create a key right here. Give it a name and copy it. It also shows up in Studio under API Keys.

Create an API key in Reducto Studio (https://studio.reducto.ai) under API Keys. Signed-in readers can create one on this page. Store it as `REDUCTO_API_KEY`.

### Set your API key as an environment variable

This allows the SDK to authenticate automatically without hardcoding the key in your code.

macOS / Linux

```sh
export REDUCTO_API_KEY="your-api-key"

```

Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
$env:REDUCTO_API_KEY = "your-api-key"

```

### Install the SDK

Choose your language and install the Reducto SDK. Python requires 3.8+.

Python

```sh
pip install reductoai

```

Node.js

```sh
npm install reductoai

```

Go

```sh
go get github.com/reductoai/reducto-go-sdk

```

## What we're going to parse

We'll use a financial statement PDF that contains multiple tables, headers, account summaries, and formatted text. This is the kind of complex document that's difficult to process manually but straightforward with Reducto.

![A Fidelity investment report with its two tables marked TABLE](https://docs.reducto.ai/brand/finance-detail.webp)

View the sample PDF in Studio or download it directly to follow along.

What we want to extract:

- The portfolio value table with beginning and ending values
- Account information including account numbers and types
- Income summary broken down by tax category
- Top holdings with values and percentages

By the end of this guide, you'll have all of this data in structured JSON that you can use in your application. For structured field extraction (e.g., extracting specific account numbers or values into typed fields), see the /extract endpoint after completing this quickstart.

---

## Parse the document

Now write the code that parses the financial statement. Here is what Reducto returns for it.

Python

```python
from pathlib import Path
from reducto import Reducto

client = Reducto()
upload = client.upload(file=Path("fidelity-example.pdf"))
result = client.parse.run(input=upload.file_id, settings={"model": "r-1"})

print(f"Processed {result.usage.num_pages} pages")

for chunk in result.result.chunks:
    print(chunk.content)
    for block in chunk.blocks:
        if block.type == "Table":
            print(f"Found table on page {block.bbox.page}")

```

# Authentication

> Understand principals, tokens, and how to authenticate with the Devin API

The Devin API uses a principal + token model. A principal is who you are (your identity), and a token is how you prove it (your credential). Understanding this distinction is the key to choosing the right authentication method for your use case.

## Principals & tokens

| Principal | Token | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Service User (non-human) | Service User API Key | For automated integrations and CI/CD pipelines |
| User (human) | Personal Access Token (PAT) | For human programmatic access under your own identity |

All API credentials use the `cog_` prefix format. Include your token in the `Authorization` header of every request:

```bash
curl -X GET "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer cog_your_token_here"

```

The key distinction is which principal the token authenticates as:

- A Service User API Key authenticates as the service user — the service user's identity, permissions, and org memberships apply.
- A Personal Access Token authenticates as the human user who created it — that user's identity, permissions, and org memberships apply.

### Personal access token or service user?

| | Personal access token | Service user API key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acts as | You | A separate non-human identity |
| Permissions | Exactly yours, in every organization you have access to | The role you give the service user, in the organizations it is added to |
| Scope | Your account. Each request names the organization | Created at the organization or enterprise level |
| Audit trail | Attributed to you | Attributed to the service user, even when it creates a session on someone's behalf with `create_as_user_id` |
| Lifecycle | Tied to you. Revoked automatically if you leave the account | Not tied to any person, so it survives team changes |
| Best for | Personal scripts, local tooling, the Devin CLI and desktop apps | CI/CD, production integrations, shared automation |

Rule of thumb: if the integration should keep working after you leave the team or change roles, use a service user. If it should do exactly what you can do, as you, use a PAT.

---

## Service users (recommended for automation)

Service users are non-human accounts designed for API integrations. They can be assigned specific permissions via RBAC and added to organizations independently of human users.

### How it works

1. Provision a service user in Settings > Devin API (Service users tab) for an organization, or Enterprise settings > Devin API (Service users tab) for the enterprise
2. Assign a role that controls which endpoints the service user can access. You pick a role from a dropdown, not individual permissions

# Devin MCP

> Set up the official Devin MCP server so external AI tools can manage sessions, playbooks, knowledge, and repository docs.

The Devin MCP server provides programmatic access to Devin's platform capabilities for both private and public repositories. Beyond repository documentation and search, it gives any MCP-compatible AI agent or IDE full access to session management, playbooks, knowledge, and scheduling.

> [!NOTE]
> 
> Any Devin session or MCP-compatible client can create sessions, manage playbooks and knowledge, set up schedules, and more. See Advanced Capabilities for details on what Devin can do.

## What is MCP?

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI apps to securely connect to MCP-compatible data sources and tools. You can think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications — a standardized way to connect AI apps to different services.

## Devin MCP Server

The Devin MCP server is an authenticated service that provides access to both public and private repositories, plus full platform management capabilities.

Base Server URL: `https://mcp.devin.ai/`

### Authentication Required

To use the Devin MCP server, you need a Devin API key:

1. Sign up for a Devin account at Devin.ai
2. Generate an API key from your account settings
3. Include the API key in your MCP client configuration

The MCP server supports the same authentication methods as the Devin API:

| Token type | Prefix | Org resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Org-scoped service user key | `cog_` | Automatic — org_id is resolved from the service user |
| Enterprise service user key | `cog_` | Requires `X-Org-Id` header (see below) |
| Personal access token | `cog_` | Requires `X-Org-Id` header (see below) |

> [!NOTE]
> 
> Legacy API keys (`apk_` / `apk_user_` prefix) only work with the repository documentation tools (`read_wiki_structure`, `read_wiki_contents`, `ask_wiki_question`, `list_wiki_repos`). The session, playbook, knowledge, schedule, and integration tools reject them because they cannot be resolved to an organization. Use a service user API key for those.

#### Enterprise accounts: `X-Org-Id` header

Enterprise service user keys and PATs are scoped to the account level, not a specific organization. Since the MCP tools operate on organization-level resources (sessions, playbooks, knowledge, etc.), you must tell the server which organization to target by passing the `X-Org-Id` header:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "devin": {
      "serverUrl": "https://mcp.devin.ai/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>",
        "X-Org-Id": "<YOUR_ORG_ID>"
      }
    }
  }
}

```

> [!TIP]
> 
> Find your organization ID at the top of the Settings > Devin API page.

Org-scoped service user keys do not need this header — the organization

> Connect a custom ticketing system to Devin with a webhook handler that calls the Devin API to start a session for each new bug ticket.

# Auto-Fix Tickets via Webhooks

Connect on-prem or unsupported ticketing systems to Devin with a webhook-to-session bridge.

Try in Devin ↗

Author
Cognition

Category
Automations

> [!TIP]
> 
> Don't want to set this up manually? Paste a link to this page into a Devin session and ask it to set everything up for you.

1. Create a service user

Devin uses service user tokens to authenticate API calls. This is the recommended approach for production automation.

1. Go to app.devin.ai > Settings > Devin API > Service users and create a new service user with a role that includes the Use Devin sessions (`UseDevinSessions`) permission — creating sessions requires this permission, and `ManageOrgSessions` alone does not grant it
2. Copy the API token shown after creation and store it securely — it's only displayed once and you'll use it as `DEVIN_API_KEY` in your webhook handler

Your organization ID is shown at the top of the Settings > Devin API page — the URL only shows the org slug, not the ID.

Test it with a quick curl:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/YOUR_ORG_ID/sessions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt": "Say hello — this is a test session."}'

```

You should get back a `session_id` and `url`. Delete the test session in the Devin web app and move on.

2. Build the webhook handler

This pattern is ideal for on-prem ticketing systems (like self-hosted Jira, Redmine, or Bugzilla) or ticketing tools that don't have a native Devin integration (unlike Linear and Jira Cloud, which have built-in support). If your ticketing system supports webhooks, you can bridge it to Devin with a small service.

Include a link to your ticketing system's API documentation in the prompt so Devin can figure out how to post comments back to tickets. Pass the ticketing API token as a session secret so Devin can authenticate directly.

Ask Devin to scaffold it:

```txt

1. Accepts POST /webhooks/tickets with a JSON body containing id, title,

2. Verifies the webhook signature using HMAC-SHA256
3. Skips tickets without a "devin-autofix" or "devin-feature" label
4. Calls POST https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/{org_id}/sessions
   with a prompt built from the ticket fields, a skill mention based on
   the label, and the ticketing API token as a session secret

Read DEVIN_API_KEY, DEVIN_ORG_ID, TICKET_API_TOKEN, and WEBHOOK_SECRET
from environment variables.

```

> ## Documentation Index
>

> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Personal Access Tokens

> Authenticate as yourself for programmatic API access

## Overview

Personal Access Tokens (PATs) allow human users to authenticate programmatically under their own identity. Unlike service user API keys (which authenticate as a non-human service user), a PAT authenticates as you — the human user who created the token.

| Token type | Authenticates as | Identity | Permissions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Service User API Key | Service User (non-human) | The service user's identity | The service user's assigned role |
| Personal Access Token | User (human) | Your user identity | Your permissions and org memberships |

All API credentials use the `cog_` prefix format. Both token types are used identically in the `Authorization` header:

```bash
curl "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $YOUR_PAT"

```

## Scope and permissions

A PAT belongs to you, within your account (your Teams account or your enterprise). It is not tied to one organization, and there is no such thing as an "organization PAT" or an "enterprise PAT". This is different from service users, which are created at either the organization or enterprise level.

| | Personal access token |
| --- | --- |
| Belongs to | Your user, within one account |
| Where you manage it | The PATs tab on Settings > Devin API, in any organization or in enterprise settings |
| What it can call | `/v3/organizations/{org_id}/*` for every organization you have access to; `/v3/enterprise/*` if you have the matching enterprise permissions |

Each request picks the organization. Organization endpoints name it in the URL path (`/v3/organizations/{org_id}/...`), and the request is authorized by your access and role in that organization. A request for an organization you can't access fails.

The token has the same permissions as your user. Anything you can do in the web app, you can do with your PAT, and nothing more.

To create, rotate, or revoke PATs you need Manage API keys in the organization whose settings you are viewing, or Manage account API keys at the account level. This permission controls who can manage tokens; it does not change what a token can do.

Enterprise accounts also have an internal organization that only stores enterprise-wide settings. It is not a workspace. PAT requests that target it are rejected with `403`, so always use a child organization ID.

## When to use PATs

PATs are designed for scenarios where you need programmatic API access as yourself:

- Personal scripts and tooling — automate your own workflows without a shared service user
- Local development — test API integrations using your own account
- Short-lived automation — one-off scripts that should be attributed to you

# API Overview

> Learn how to programmatically interact with Devin using our REST APIs

The Devin API enables you to integrate Devin into your applications, automate workflows, and build powerful tools. Use service users with role-based access control for secure, auditable API access.

## Getting started

> [card] Teams quick start
> 
> For teams and standard organizations. Create a service user and make your first API call in minutes.

> [card] Enterprise quick start
> 
> For enterprise customers with RBAC, multi-org support, and advanced permissions.

> [!TIP]
> 
> Which path should I choose? Most customers should start with the Teams quick start. Choose Enterprise if you manage multiple organizations or need custom roles and RBAC.

## API structure

The API is organized into two scopes:

### Organization API

Base URL: `https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/*`

For managing resources within a single organization — sessions, knowledge, playbooks, secrets, and more. This is where most integrations start.

### Enterprise API

Base URL: `https://api.devin.ai/v3/enterprise/*`

For cross-organization management — analytics, audit logs, user management, billing, and infrastructure. Available to enterprise customers.

Both scopes use service user credentials (`cog_` prefix). See Authentication for setup.

## Session attribution

Service users are separate identities from human users, but you can create sessions on behalf of any user in your organization using the `create_as_user_id` parameter. This means sessions appear in that user's session list and count toward their usage — just like they created it themselves.

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "prompt": "Fix the login bug in issue #42",
    "create_as_user_id": "user_abc123"
  }'

```

> [!TIP]
> 
> Coming from personal API keys? In v1/v2, personal API keys automatically created sessions as your user. With v3, use a service user + `create_as_user_id` for the same behavior — with the added benefit of RBAC, audit trails, and centralized key management. The service user's role must include `ImpersonateOrgSessions` permission.

> [!NOTE]
> 
> You can also authenticate directly as your user with a Personal Access Token — no service user or `create_as_user_id` needed. Sessions are automatically attributed to you.

You can find user IDs with the List organization users endpoint (beta, organization-scoped service user) or the enterprise List users endpoint. Both return only users with direct role assignments. For users whose membership comes from IDP groups, use List organization IDP group users or its enterprise equivalent.

# Authentication

> Authenticate server-side API requests with your Higgsfield key and secret.

Create and manage API credentials in Higgsfield Console. Each credential consists of a key ID and a secret.

## Authorization header

Send both values in the `Authorization` header:

```http
Authorization: Key YOUR_KEY_ID:YOUR_KEY_SECRET

```

```bash
curl https://api.higgsfield.ai/requests/REQUEST_ID/status \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}"

```

The API also accepts the legacy `hf-api-key` and `hf-secret` headers. New integrations should use the `Authorization` header.

## Keep credentials server-side

> [!WARNING]
> 
> Do not call the API directly from browser or mobile application code. Anyone who can inspect the application can extract its API secret and use your account.

- Store credentials in a secrets manager or encrypted environment variables.
- Use separate credentials for development and production.
- Never include credentials in URLs, logs, screenshots, or support messages.
- Rotate a credential immediately if it may have been exposed.

## Authentication errors

Missing, malformed, or invalid credentials return `401 Unauthorized`:

```json
{
  "detail": "Invalid credentials"
}

```

Authentication identifies the account, but individual models may have separate access restrictions. A model unavailable to the authenticated account can return `404`, `423`, or `503` depending on its operational state.

# Webhooks

> Receive terminal generation results without continuous polling.

Pass an HTTPS endpoint in the `hf_webhook` query parameter when submitting generation. Higgsfield sends one or more HTTP `POST` deliveries after the request reaches `completed`, `failed`, or `nsfw`.

## Configure a webhook

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url "https://api.higgsfield.ai/higgsfield-ai/soul/v2/standard?hf_webhook=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fwebhooks%2Fhiggsfield" \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "prompt": "Editorial portrait in soft daylight"
  }'

```

Your endpoint must be publicly reachable over HTTPS, accept a JSON request body, and respond within ten seconds.

## Payload envelope

All deliveries use the same top-level envelope. Successful output is nested in `payload`.

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "completed",
  "error": null,
  "expires_at": "2026-10-31T12:05:12.481Z",
  "payload": {
    "images": [
      {
        "url": "https://cdn.example.com/generated-image.jpg",
        "content_type": "image/jpeg"
      }
    ]
  }
}

```

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "completed",
  "error": null,
  "payload": {
    "video": {
      "url": "https://cdn.example.com/generated-video.mp4",
      "content_type": "video/mp4"
    }
  }
}

```

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "failed",
  "error": "Generation failed",
  "payload": null
}

```

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "nsfw",
  "error": null,
  "payload": null
}

```

Audio responses contain `payload.audio`. Some video and 3D operations can also include `zip`, `mov`, `jsx`, `fbx`, or `ply` artifacts.

`expires_at` is the time after which the request's files are deleted and the URLs in `payload` stop working; download them before then. See Data retention and deletion.

## Verify signatures

Webhook deliveries are signed using the Standard Webhooks specification. Verify every delivery before trusting its contents: anyone who knows your endpoint URL can send it a request.

Each signed delivery includes three headers:

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `webhook-id` | Unique event identifier. It stays the same across retries of the same event. |
| `webhook-timestamp` | Unix time in seconds when the delivery was signed. |
| `webhook-signature` | One or more space-separated signatures in the form `v1,`. |

### Get your signing secret

Open Settings in Higgsfield Console and reveal the webhook signing secret. It starts with `whsec_`. The secret is created the first time it is revealed; until then, deliveries for your account are not signed.

# Higgsfield API

> Generate images and videos through one authenticated, asynchronous API.

Higgsfield provides one integration point for generative media models. Submit a request to a model endpoint, then poll for the result or receive a webhook when processing finishes.

> [card] Run your first request
> 
> Create credentials and complete a generation from submission to result.

> [card] Get an API key
> 
> Create and manage server-side credentials in Higgsfield Console.

## Make a request

Every model uses the same authentication and asynchronous request lifecycle. The JSON body depends on the selected model.

Start with Genjutsu motion transfer. Replace the example media URLs with publicly accessible URLs for your own video and reference image. The source video must be at least 4 seconds long.

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.higgsfield.ai/higgsfield/genjutsu/motion-transfer/v1.0 \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "video_url": "https://example.com/input.mp4",
    "image_urls": ["https://example.com/input.jpg"]
  }'

```

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.higgsfield.ai/higgsfield-ai/soul/v2/standard \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "prompt": "Editorial portrait in soft daylight"
  }'

```

The API immediately returns a request identifier and links for checking or canceling the request.

```json
{
  "status": "queued",
  "request_id": "d7e6c0f3-6699-4f6c-bb45-2ad7fd9158ff",
  "status_url": "https://api.higgsfield.ai/requests/d7e6c0f3-6699-4f6c-bb45-2ad7fd9158ff/status",
  "cancel_url": "https://api.higgsfield.ai/requests/d7e6c0f3-6699-4f6c-bb45-2ad7fd9158ff/cancel"
}

```

## Choose your path

> [card] Build a prototype
> 
> Use the Python or TypeScript SDK to submit a request and wait for its result.

> [card] Ship to production
> 
> Learn the request lifecycle, polling, webhooks, errors, and limits.

> [card] Upload media
> 
> Upload input files to Higgsfield storage before generation.

> [!NOTE]
> 
> Output files are available for at least seven days. Download completed output to your own storage for long-term retention.

## Related topics

- Enterprise API
- How the API works
- Model API Reference
- Genjutsu API

> ## Documentation Index

# Enterprise API

> Data controls, security, capacity and support for production integrations at scale.

The Higgsfield API gives every account the same endpoints. This section collects the controls that matter when you run it in production for an organization: where your data lives and for how long, who can access the API, how much capacity you get, how usage is reported, and how to reach us when something goes wrong.

> [card] Data retention and deletion
> 
> Keep request inputs and outputs for as little as one hour, or delete a request on demand.

> [card] Model training opt-out
> 
> Exclude your inputs and generated outputs from model training.

> [card] Webhook security
> 
> Verify that every delivery comes from Higgsfield and was not modified.

> [card] Organizations and roles
> 
> What an organization shares, and what admins and members can do.

> [card] Access control
> 
> SAML single sign-on, organization roles and API key lifecycle.

> [card] Capacity and concurrency
> 
> How limits work, what happens at the limit and how to get more capacity.

> [card] Usage and billing
> 
> Usage analytics in USD and invoice billing.

> [card] Reliability and support
> 
> Status page, incident communication, support and SLAs.

## At a glance

| Area | What you get | Where to configure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data retention | Inputs and outputs deleted after 1 hour to 7 days; delete any finished request immediately | `Hf-Expires-After` header, account setting, `DELETE /requests/{request_id}` |
| Model training | Inputs and generated outputs excluded from training | Settings in Higgsfield Console |
| Webhooks | Standard Webhooks signatures with secret rotation | Settings in Higgsfield Console |
| Identity | SAML SSO (Okta, Microsoft, custom), Admin and Member roles with a permission matrix | Organization settings |
| API keys | Named keys with expiration, tags and last-used time | API keys in Higgsfield Console |
| Capacity | Account and model concurrency; requests above the limit are queued | Higgsfield Console; higher or dedicated capacity on request |
| Usage analytics | Per-model usage and estimated cost in USD, for dashboards and monitoring | `GET /models/usage`, Higgsfield Console |
| Reliability | Public status page, correlation IDs for every response | status.higgsfield.ai |

> [!NOTE]
> 
> Some settings, such as an account-wide retention period, invoice billing and dedicated capacity, are configured by Higgsfield. Email support@higgsfield.ai or contact your account manager.

## Related topics

- Access control
- Organizations and roles
- Reliability and support
- Usage and billing
- Data retention and deletion

```http
Authorization: Key YOUR_KEY_ID:YOUR_KEY_SECRET

```

```bash
curl https://api.higgsfield.ai/requests/REQUEST_ID/status \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}"

```

The API also accepts the legacy `hf-api-key` and `hf-secret` headers. New integrations should use the `Authorization` header.

## Keep credentials server-side

> [!WARNING]
> 
> Do not call the API directly from browser or mobile application code. Anyone who can inspect the application can extract its API secret and use your account.

- Store credentials in a secrets manager or encrypted environment variables.
- Use separate credentials for development and production.
- Never include credentials in URLs, logs, screenshots, or support messages.
- Rotate a credential immediately if it may have been exposed.

## Authentication errors

Missing, malformed, or invalid credentials return `401 Unauthorized`:

```json
{
  "detail": "Invalid credentials"
}

```

Authentication identifies the account, but individual models may have separate access restrictions. A model unavailable to the authenticated account can return `404`, `423`, or `503` depending on its operational state.

> ## Documentation Index
> 
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.higgsfield.ai/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Webhooks

> Receive terminal generation results without continuous polling.

Pass an HTTPS endpoint in the `hf_webhook` query parameter when submitting generation. Higgsfield sends one or more HTTP `POST` deliveries after the request reaches `completed`, `failed`, or `nsfw`.

## Configure a webhook

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url "https://api.higgsfield.ai/higgsfield-ai/soul/v2/standard?hf_webhook=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fwebhooks%2Fhiggsfield" \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "prompt": "Editorial portrait in soft daylight"
  }'

```

Your endpoint must be publicly reachable over HTTPS, accept a JSON request body, and respond within ten seconds.

## Payload envelope

All deliveries use the same top-level envelope. Successful output is nested in `payload`.

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "completed",
  "error": null,
  "expires_at": "2026-10-31T12:05:12.481Z",
  "payload": {
    "images": [
      {
        "url": "https://cdn.example.com/generated-image.jpg",
        "content_type": "image/jpeg"
      }
    ]
  }
}

```

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "completed",
  "error": null,
  "payload": {
    "video": {
      "url": "https://cdn.example.com/generated-video.mp4",
      "content_type": "video/mp4"
    }
  }
}

```

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "failed",
  "error": "Generation failed",
  "payload": null
}

```

```json
{
  "request_id": "9417a243-e457-4075-895b-b68f3cda5303",
  "status": "nsfw",
  "error": null,
  "payload": null
}

```

Audio responses contain `payload.audio`. Some video and 3D operations can also include `zip`, `mov`, `jsx`, `fbx`, or `ply` artifacts.

`expires_at` is the time after which the request's files are deleted and the URLs in `payload` stop working; download them before then. See Data retention and deletion.

## Verify signatures

Webhook deliveries are signed using the Standard Webhooks specification. Verify every delivery before trusting its contents: anyone who knows your endpoint URL can send it a request.

Each signed delivery includes three headers:

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `webhook-id` | Unique event identifier. It stays the same across retries of the same event. |
| `webhook-timestamp` | Unix time in seconds when the delivery was signed. |
| `webhook-signature` | One or more space-separated signatures in the form `v1,`. |

### Get your signing secret

Open Settings in Higgsfield Console and reveal the webhook signing secret. It starts with `whsec_`. The secret is created the first time it is revealed; until then, deliveries for your account are not signed.

# Higgsfield API

> Generate images and videos through one authenticated, asynchronous API.

Higgsfield provides one integration point for generative media models. Submit a request to a model endpoint, then poll for the result or receive a webhook when processing finishes.

> [card] Run your first request
> 
> Create credentials and complete a generation from submission to result.

> [card] Get an API key
> 
> Create and manage server-side credentials in Higgsfield Console.

## Make a request

Every model uses the same authentication and asynchronous request lifecycle. The JSON body depends on the selected model.

Start with Genjutsu motion transfer. Replace the example media URLs with publicly accessible URLs for your own video and reference image. The source video must be at least 4 seconds long.

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.higgsfield.ai/higgsfield/genjutsu/motion-transfer/v1.0 \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "video_url": "https://example.com/input.mp4",
    "image_urls": ["https://example.com/input.jpg"]
  }'

```

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.higgsfield.ai/higgsfield-ai/soul/v2/standard \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "prompt": "Editorial portrait in soft daylight"
  }'

```

The API immediately returns a request identifier and links for checking or canceling the request.

```json
{
  "status": "queued",
  "request_id": "d7e6c0f3-6699-4f6c-bb45-2ad7fd9158ff",
  "status_url": "https://api.higgsfield.ai/requests/d7e6c0f3-6699-4f6c-bb45-2ad7fd9158ff/status",
  "cancel_url": "https://api.higgsfield.ai/requests/d7e6c0f3-6699-4f6c-bb45-2ad7fd9158ff/cancel"
}

```

## Choose your path

> [card] Build a prototype
> 
> Use the Python or TypeScript SDK to submit a request and wait for its result.

> [card] Ship to production
> 
> Learn the request lifecycle, polling, webhooks, errors, and limits.

> [card] Upload media
> 
> Upload input files to Higgsfield storage before generation.

> [!NOTE]
> 
> Output files are available for at least seven days. Download completed output to your own storage for long-term retention.

> ## Documentation Index
> 
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.higgsfield.ai/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Billing and retention

> Understand charging, refunds, estimation, and output retention.

Higgsfield charges successful generation requests to your account balance. The exact cost depends on the selected model and parameters.

## Balance expiration

Funds added to your account balance expire one year after they are added. Plan purchases and usage with this expiration period in mind.

## Estimate a request

Use the estimate endpoint with the same model parameters before submitting generation:

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.higgsfield.ai/estimate/higgsfield-ai/soul/v2/standard \
  --header "Authorization: Key ${HF_API_KEY_ID}:${HF_API_KEY_SECRET}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "prompt": "Editorial portrait in soft daylight"
  }'

```

```json
{
  "usd": "0.094"
}

```

> [!NOTE]
> 
> The values above illustrate the response format. Use the estimate returned for your authenticated account as the authoritative amount.

## Failed and moderated requests

Requests ending as `failed` or `nsfw` are not charged. If an amount was reserved when the request was accepted, it is refunded automatically.

## Canceled requests

A request can be canceled only before processing starts. A successfully canceled queued request is refunded.

## Output retention

Request files are kept for seven days after the request finishes, then deleted. The status response and the webhook include `expires_at`, the time of deletion. Download completed files to your own storage for long-term retention.

To keep data for less time, send the `Hf-Expires-After` header (one hour or more) or ask Higgsfield to set a retention period for your account. To remove a finished request immediately, call `DELETE /requests/{request_id}`. Billing records are kept in both cases. See Data retention and deletion.

## Related topics

- Data retention and deletion
- FAQ

- Delete request data
- Usage and billing

name: mermaid-api
description: Validate and render Mermaid diagrams to SVG, PNG, PDF or ASCII text through the hosted Mermaid API, with curl. Use when checking Mermaid syntax, turning diagram code into an image file, generating or repairing a diagram with Mermaid AI, listing projects and diagrams, creating, fetching, updating or sharing stored Mermaid Chart diagrams, or setting up a Mermaid API key.
---

# Mermaid API

Mermaid API validates and renders Mermaid diagrams over HTTP, and asks Mermaid
AI to generate or repair diagram code. It is in beta: fields, limits and the
latest Mermaid version can change, so tell the user not to build a production
dependency on it.

Every call below is plain `curl` from the shell. Start every command with this
preamble; shell variables do not carry over between your commands. It sets the
base URL (`MERMAID_API_URL` overrides production) and the key header, explained
under Key:

```bash
api=${MERMAID_API_URL:-https://api.mermaid.ai}
if [ -n "$MERMAID_API_KEY" ]; then auth=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $MERMAID_API_KEY"); else auth=(-H @"$HOME/.config/mermaid-api/credentials"); fi
```

## Key

The key stays out of sight: it reaches curl only through shell expansion, so
its value never appears in the chat, a command line or the project. Treat
`$MERMAID_API_KEY` and the credentials file as write-only: never print, `cat`,
`echo` or read them.

Resolve it in this order, and send it as the matching header:

1. `MERMAID_API_KEY` set:
 `-H "Authorization: Bearer $MERMAID_API_KEY"`.
2. Otherwise `~/.config/mermaid-api/credentials`, which holds the whole header
 line: `-H @"$HOME/.config/mermaid-api/credentials"` (`@~/…` does not
 expand).

### Setup

When neither resolves
(`[ -n "$MERMAID_API_KEY" ] || [ -s ~/.config/mermaid-api/credentials ]`
fails), curl exits 26 because the credentials file is missing, or a call answers
`ERR_KEY_MISSING`:

1. Send the user to `$api/console` to create a key. It is shown once.
2. Give them this to run **in their own terminal**, not through you. It prompts
 for the key without echoing it, in bash or zsh, and writes the file with mode
 0600:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/.config/mermaid-api && (umask 077; printf 'Mermaid API key: '; read -rs k && printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' "$k" > ~/.config/mermaid-api/credentials; echo)
   ```

3. When they say it is done, confirm with `GET /v1/balance`, which is free.
 Setup is done when it answers 200.

## Endpoints

Costs are in API credits, charged to the key owner's balance.

| Endpoint | Use it to | Cost |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| `POST /v1/validate` | Check diagram code; on invalid code it gives the parser's line and column | 1 |
| `POST /v1/render` | Turn diagram code into SVG, PNG, PDF or ASCII text | 5 |
| `POST /v1/generate` | Ask Mermaid AI for d

# Simple steps to test this locally

```
registry=https://registry.npmjs.com/
```

Instead of creating a .npmrc file on your own you can also use npm login --registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com which gives you an interactive prompt for entering your credentials.

1. Do `npm install`

```sh
npm install
```

2. Run the script like below:

```sh
node src/cli.js -i test-positive/state1.mmd
```
